opus-5.5.text:
I think what draws me to product-oriented ideas is that they force you to be honest about whether you're actually solving a problem. In research, especially in reinforcement learning or large-model infrastructure, it's very easy to optimize for something that looks good on a benchmark or in a paper, but nobody outside a small circle really feels the difference. With a product, the feedback loop is brutal and immediate: either people use it, come back, and tell their friends, or they don't. There's no hiding behind a nice plot.

The other part is that I've always enjoyed building things end to end. When I worked on Tianshou, for example, the most satisfying moments weren't when we hit some number, but when someone I'd never met opened an issue saying, "I used this for my thesis," or "this saved me weeks." That's a product feeling, even though it was an open-source library. You start thinking about the user's first five minutes, the documentation, the error messages, the boring stuff that actually decides whether something gets adopted.

And honestly, right now, with how capable models have become, the bottleneck has shifted. The raw capability is increasingly there; what's scarce is figuring out the right interface, the right workflow, the thing that makes that capability actually useful in someone's daily life. That's a product question, not purely a technical one. So for me, product-oriented startup ideas are where the technical depth and the real-world impact meet, and that intersection is where I find the work most meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response describes immediate user feedback and mentions a Tianshou user reporting that it helped with a thesis, but it does not say that researcher feedback enables real-time iteration on research infrastructure.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what draws me in is that product-oriented ideas force you to be honest about whether something actually matters to a real person. When I was doing research, you could spend months on something, get a nice number on a benchmark, and never really know whether anyone would use it. With a product, the feedback loop is brutal and fast. Either someone opens it a second time or they don't.

There's also a craft element I enjoy. Most infrastructure problems don't come with a clear answer, you kind of have to feel your way through them. With a product, you can start from a very specific pain point, often your own, and work backwards. Like, I'm annoyed that this takes five steps, can I make it take one? That constraint is clarifying. It tells you what to build and, more importantly, what not to build.

And honestly, the thing I find most appealing is that small teams can do it now. A lot of the heavy lifting that used to need a big infra team, you can get from models and APIs today. So the bottleneck has shifted from "can we build this" to "do we understand the user well enough." That's a much more interesting question to me, and it's one where a tiny, fast-moving team can actually beat a large company.

r001.rationale: The response describes fast user feedback for products, but does not say that researchers’ use of research infrastructure enables real-time iteration on that infrastructure.

You can start with a problem, build a small solution, and learn from how people respond. I like that feedback loop—you’re constantly testing your assumptions and making the product more useful. And there’s something really satisfying about creating something that becomes part of someone’s everyday life.
